angle-1.label: It's Not Your System

angle-1.label: Authority Without Access

angle-1.label: IT Becomes the Comp Team

angle-2.label: Held Hostage by IT

angle-2.label: Permanently Reactive

angle-1.expansion: You can't move the business forward when your bandwidth is consumed proving the current state wrong. Your strategic value is invisible as long as you're in cleanup mode.

angle-2.label: Black Box Dependency
angle-2.expansion: You're supposed to own the comp plan — but you can't read it. Every change, every audit, every question routes through a consultant you have to pay to understand your own system.

angle-2.label: Audit Exposure Without Defense
angle-2.expansion: When a rep disputes their payout or finance asks how the plan calculates, you're presenting code you didn't write and can't explain. You become the face of logic you've never actually seen.

angle-2.label: Expertise Made Invisible
angle-2.expansion: You built your career knowing comp inside out. The platform turned that expertise into a support ticket — the consultant is the expert now, not you.

angle-1.label: Admin In Name Only
angle-1.expansion: You have 'administrator' in your title but can't administer anything without filing a ticket. Every config change is a reminder that you don't actually own your own system.

angle-1.label: Held Hostage by IT
angle-1.expansion: When the business moves and comp needs to follow, you're waiting on a queue. Your credibility as a comp leader depends on a team whose priorities were never your plan.

angle-1.label: Every Change Has a Tax
angle-1.expansion: A quota update, a new accelerator, a mid-year realignment — each one costs you days you don't have. The platform is supposed to reduce your workload, not multiply it.

angle-3.label: Designing Around the Tool
angle-3.expansion: When you avoid changes because of what they'll cost you in PS tickets and wait time, the tool is making your comp decisions. You're not.

angle-3.label: Strategy Becomes Compromise
angle-3.expansion: You can't tell your CFO the plan reflects business logic when half the structure exists because it was easier to leave alone. You're defending inertia, not intent.

angle-3.label: Admin in Title Only
angle-3.expansion: You're accountable for how the plan performs, but you need a vendor's approval and a two-week queue to change it. That's not ownership — that's liability without control.

angle-1.label: Credibility on the Clock
angle-1.expansion: Every week reps wait for accurate statements, they're not questioning the delay — they're questioning you. You become the face of a system that can't keep up.

angle-1.label: Payroll Held Hostage
angle-1.expansion: When the validation cycle owns your calendar, you're not running comp — you're chasing it. The quarter doesn't close when the business closes. It closes when your spreadsheet lets it.

angle-1.label: Trust Bleeds Per Cycle
angle-1.expansion: Reps who wait weeks for accurate pay stop trusting the number when it finally arrives. You've lost the moment where comp was supposed to motivate — and there's no recovering it mid-quarter.

angle-2.label: Trust You Can't Rebuild
angle-2.expansion: When reps wait until May to see Q1 money, they stop believing the system works — and they start believing you don't care. That skepticism doesn't reset when the check finally arrives.

angle-2.label: Messenger for Someone Else's Failure
angle-2.expansion: The system caused the delay. You're the one in the all-hands explaining it. Every town hall where you defend a two-month lag is credibility you spent on a problem you didn't create.

angle-2.label: Comp as Retention Tool, Gone
angle-2.expansion: Commissions are supposed to be the reason reps stay through a hard quarter. When the payout arrives two months late, it doesn't reinforce the win — it just confirms the dysfunction.

angle-1.label: Execution Ceiling
angle-1.expansion: You can architect the perfect plan change in an afternoon. But you can't execute it without burning three days on 55 identical edits — the system caps what you're capable of.

angle-1.label: You Delay the Business
angle-1.expansion: Sales leadership calls for a mid-quarter adjustment. You're the reason it takes a week. Not because you're slow — because your tools make scale impossible.

angle-1.label: Reduced to Data Entry
angle-1.expansion: You built expertise to design comp strategy — not to manually touch 55 records every time the business pivots. The tool turns a comp professional into a data entry clerk.

angle-2.label: Architect Reduced to Typist
angle-2.expansion: You were hired to design comp strategy. Instead, you're manually re-entering logic you already built last quarter. The system treats your expertise as if it doesn't exist.

angle-2.label: Scale Blocked by the Tool
angle-2.expansion: Every new segment your sales org adds is a project you have to justify resourcing. Growth shouldn't require you to rebuild from zero — but your system makes it a personal tax.

angle-2.label: Error Surface Multiplies With You
angle-2.expansion: Every manual recode is another place a logic drift can hide. When a discrepancy surfaces, you can't prove which version of the plan is authoritative — because none of them share a source.

angle-1.label: Shadow System Tax
angle-1.expansion: You're maintaining two versions of reality — and the sandbox is already drifting from prod. Every test you run is against a environment you no longer fully trust.

angle-1.label: Launch Day Exposure
angle-1.expansion: When deployment day comes, you're not confident — you're hoping. The gap between what you tested and what goes live is where your credibility lives.

angle-1.label: Complexity You Inherited
angle-1.expansion: The sandbox wasn't your idea, but the coordination overhead is yours to carry. You became the person who manages the tool that manages the tool.

angle-2.label: Operator, Not Architect
angle-2.expansion: You were hired to design incentive strategy. Instead, you're spending full days configuring a single spiff — the system turned a strategic role into a data entry job.

angle-2.label: You Can't Move at Sales Speed
angle-2.expansion: When the field needs a promo live by Monday, a full-day setup cycle means you're the reason it's late — not the plan, not the budget. You.

angle-2.label: Every Test Is a Confession
angle-2.expansion: A day of testing before you go live tells everyone the system can't be trusted on first pass — and neither, by extension, can you.

angle-2.label: Knowledge Held Hostage
angle-2.expansion: The consultant knows your comp system better than you do. That's not a vendor relationship — that's a dependency you can't afford to admit out loud.

angle-2.label: Admin In Name Only
angle-2.expansion: Your title says you own comp operations. But every change request that routes through a consultant proves you don't. You're approving work you can't do yourself.

angle-2.label: Single Point of Failure
angle-2.expansion: When the consultant is unavailable and a plan needs to change, the answer is 'we have to wait.' You're the one delivering that answer to leadership.

angle-1.label: Budget Held Hostage
angle-1.expansion: Every change that should take you an afternoon now requires a purchase order. You're not running a comp program — you're managing a vendor relationship that never ends.

angle-1.label: Competence Questioned by Proxy
angle-1.expansion: When your team can't make a plan change without calling in outside help, the unspoken question in every leadership meeting is: why do we need them if the system needs consultants anyway?

angle-1.label: Change Velocity Tax
angle-1.expansion: The business moves. Your plans need to move with it. But every mid-cycle adjustment carries a billing event — so you start making fewer changes, and the comp plan slowly stops reflecting reality.
